mendelian-genetics-s1.title: A family with a rare trait
mendelian-genetics-s1.text: The pedigree shows three generations of a family in which some members have a rare condition caused by one gene. II-4 married into the family and has no relatives with the condition. Use A for the allele that does not cause the condition and a for the allele that does.

mendelian-genetics-s2.title: Kernels on an ear of corn
mendelian-genetics-s2.text: Each kernel on an ear of corn is a seed, the offspring of one fertilization. A true-breeding plant grown from purple, smooth kernels was crossed with a true-breeding plant grown from yellow, wrinkled kernels. Every F1 kernel was purple and smooth. F1 plants were then self-pollinated, and students counted the F2 kernels on one ear. Kernel color and kernel texture are each controlled by one gene, on different chromosome pairs.

table.caption: F2 kernels on one ear, by color and texture

items.q: Which mode of inheritance is most consistent with the pedigree, and which individual's phenotype rules out X-linked recessive inheritance?
options: Autosomal recessive; III-1 is an affected daughter of an unaffected father, II-4.
Autosomal dominant; II-1 is affected even though both of his parents are unaffected.
X-linked recessive; II-1, an affected son, has a mother who does not show the trait.
Autosomal recessive; II-1 is an affected son of an unaffected mother, I-2.

why.correct: Unaffected parents (I-1 and I-2; II-3 and II-4) have affected children, so the allele is recessive. A daughter with an X-linked recessive trait needs an affected father, because he gives her his only X; III-1's father is unaffected, so the gene is on an autosome.
options: Affected children of unaffected parents point to recessive; an affected daughter of an unaffected father rules out X-linked recessive.
A dominant trait shows in anyone carrying the allele, so an affected child of two unaffected parents argues against dominant inheritance.
II-1 fits X-linked recessive, but III-1 does not: her father would have to be affected.
An affected son of an unaffected mother fits both autosomal and X-linked recessive, so it does not rule out X-linkage.

items.q: Select every individual who must be heterozygous (Aa).
options: II-2
II-3
II-4
III-3

why.correct: Each unaffected parent of an affected child must carry one a allele: I-1 and I-2 (parents of II-1) and II-3 and II-4 (parents of III-1). II-2 and III-3 are unaffected children of two carriers and could be AA or Aa.
options: I-1 is unaffected but has an affected son, so he passed on an a allele: Aa.
I-2 is unaffected but has an affected son: Aa.
II-2 is unaffected (not aa), but he may have received A from both parents: AA or Aa.
II-3 is unaffected but has an affected daughter: Aa.
II-4 is unaffected but has an affected daughter, so despite no family history he carries a: Aa.
III-3 could be AA or Aa; nothing in the pedigree decides it.

items.q: What is the probability that II-2 is a carrier (Aa)? Give a decimal to two places.

why.correct: His parents are both Aa, so their children are AA, Aa, Aa or aa with equal chances. II-2 is unaffected, which removes aa and leaves three equally likely outcomes, two of them Aa: 2/3 ≈ 0.67.

items.q: II-3 and II-4 plan another child. What is the probability that the child is a boy with the condition? Give a decimal to three places.

why.correct: Aa × Aa gives aa with probability 1/4. Being a boy has probability 1/2, independently. Product rule: 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8 = 0.125.

items.q: III-3 has a child with a man who has the condition. What is the probability that this child has the condition? Give a decimal to two places.

why.correct: III-3 is unaffected with Aa × Aa parents, so she is Aa with probability 2/3. The man is aa. If she is Aa, a child is aa with probability 1/2; if she is AA, never. Product rule: 2/3 × 1/2 = 1/3 ≈ 0.33.

items.q: Which alleles are dominant?
options: The purple allele and the smooth allele
The yellow allele and the wrinkled allele
The purple allele and the wrinkled allele
The yellow allele and the smooth allele

why.correct: The F1 kernels were heterozygous for both genes and showed purple and smooth, so those alleles are dominant.
options: A heterozygote shows the dominant phenotype: the F1 were purple and smooth.
Yellow and wrinkled disappeared in the F1 and returned in the F2: they are recessive.
Wrinkled was hidden in the heterozygous F1, so it is recessive.
Yellow was hidden in the heterozygous F1, so it is recessive.

items.q: Considering color alone, calculate the ratio of purple to yellow F2 kernels, as the number of purple kernels per yellow kernel. Give one decimal place.

why.correct: Purple: 216 + 79 = 295. Yellow: 70 + 25 = 95. 295 ÷ 95 = 3.1, close to the 3:1 of a monohybrid cross.

items.q: If the two genes assort independently, how many of the 390 F2 kernels would you predict to be yellow and wrinkled? Give a whole number.

why.correct: Yellow and wrinkled is the double recessive class, 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16 of the F2. 390 ÷ 16 = 24.4, about 24 kernels (25 were counted).

items.q: The F2 counts are close to a 9:3:3:1 ratio. Which explanation connects that ratio to events in the F1 plants' meiosis?
options: The two genes' chromosome pairs line up independently at metaphase I, so PS, Ps, pS and ps gametes form in equal numbers and combine at random.
Homologs pair and swap pieces in each meiosis, which makes the four kernel types appear in a 9:3:3:1 ratio.
The purple and smooth alleles are dominant, so they go into 9 out of 16 gametes and the recessive alleles into the rest.
Each F1 plant makes two kinds of gamete, PS and ps, and their random combination at fertilization gives 9:3:3:1.

why.correct: Each F1 is PpSs. Segregation gives each gamete one allele of each gene, and because the two pairs assort independently, the four combinations are equally likely (1/4 each). Random fertilization of 4 × 4 gamete types gives 16 equally likely boxes: 9 P_S_, 3 P_ss, 3 ppS_, 1 ppss.
options: Independent assortment makes four equal gamete types; 4 × 4 random combinations give 9:3:3:1.
The ratio comes from independent assortment of separate chromosome pairs; crossing over affects genes on the same chromosome.
Dominance decides what the offspring look like, not which alleles enter gametes; each allele goes into half the gametes.
Only two gamete types would give a 3:1 pattern of purple smooth to yellow wrinkled, with no purple wrinkled or yellow smooth kernels.

items.q: A student grows a plant from one purple, smooth F2 kernel and wants to know its genotype. Which cross and result would show that it is PpSs?
options: Cross it with a plant from a yellow, wrinkled kernel; find the four phenotypes in about equal numbers.
Cross it with a plant from a purple, smooth kernel; find purple, smooth offspring and no other kind.
Cross it with a plant from a yellow, wrinkled kernel; find purple, smooth offspring and no others.
Self-pollinate it; find purple, smooth and yellow, wrinkled kernels in a 3:1 ratio.

why.correct: A testcross to ppss means every offspring gets p and s from that parent, so the offspring show directly which alleles the tested plant's gametes carried. PpSs makes PS, Ps, pS and ps equally, giving a 1:1:1:1 ratio.
options: In a testcross the offspring phenotypes mirror the tested plant's gametes: four equal classes mean PpSs.
Another purple, smooth parent can hide recessive alleles, so the result would not reveal the genotype.
Offspring that are purple and smooth every time would mean the plant is PPSS, not PpSs.
Selfing PpSs gives four phenotypes in a 9:3:3:1 ratio, not 3:1.

items.q: Two plants with genotype AaBbCc are crossed; the three genes assort independently. The chance that an offspring is aabbcc is 1 in how many? Give a whole number.

why.correct: For each gene, Aa × Aa gives aa with probability 1/4. Product rule: 1/4 × 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/64, so 1 in 64.

items.q: In a cross AaBb × Aabb (genes on different chromosome pairs; A and B dominant), what proportion of offspring are expected to show both dominant traits? Give a decimal to three places.

why.correct: Aa × Aa: dominant phenotype (AA or Aa) with probability 3/4. Bb × bb: Bb with probability 1/2. Product rule: 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8 = 0.375.

items.q: Two parents are both carriers of cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive condition. What is the probability that their next child neither has cystic fibrosis nor is a carrier?

why.correct: Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff and ff, each 1/4. Only FF is neither affected nor a carrier: 1/4.
options: FF is one of four equally likely outcomes.
1/2 is the chance of being a carrier (Ff).
3/4 is the chance of being unaffected (FF or Ff), which includes carriers.
2/3 is the chance that an unaffected child is a carrier, a different question.

items.q: In guinea pigs, black fur (B) is dominant to white (b). A black guinea pig is crossed with a white one, and the litters include 7 black and 6 white offspring. What is the black parent's genotype?
options: Bb, heterozygous
BB, homozygous dominant
bb, homozygous recessive
Unknown, since BB and Bb both look black

why.correct: White offspring are bb, so each got a b from the black parent as well as from the white one. The black parent is Bb, and Bb × bb predicts a 1:1 ratio, close to 7:6.
options: White offspring prove the black parent carries b; a 1:1 ratio fits Bb × bb.
A BB parent would give only Bb offspring, all black.
A bb guinea pig would be white, not black.
This testcross does decide it: one white offspring is enough to show the black parent carries b.

items.q: Red-green color blindness is X-linked recessive. A color-blind man has children with a woman who has normal vision but whose father was color-blind. What is expected among their children?
options: Half of their sons and half of their daughters are color-blind.
Half of their sons are color-blind, and their daughters have normal vision.
Their sons have normal vision, and half of their daughters are color-blind.
One quarter of their children are color-blind, and those are sons.

why.correct: Her father gave her his X with the allele, so she is X<sup>B</sup>X<sup>b</sup>. The man is X<sup>b</sup>Y. Sons get Y from him and either X from her: 1/2 X<sup>b</sup>Y. Daughters get his X<sup>b</sup> and either of hers: 1/2 X<sup>b</sup>X<sup>b</sup>.
options: Mother X<sup>B</sup>X<sup>b</sup> × father X<sup>b</sup>Y gives color-blind sons and daughters, half of each.
Every daughter receives the father's X<sup>b</sup>, so a daughter is color-blind whenever her mother also passes X<sup>b</sup> (half the time).
Sons get their X from the mother, who passes X<sup>b</sup> half the time.
One quarter is the result for a carrier mother and an unaffected father, not a color-blind father.

items.q: Why are X-linked recessive conditions such as hemophilia much more common in males than in females?
options: A male's single X has no partner, so one recessive allele shows; a female needs two.
The Y chromosome carries a dominant allele that switches the condition on in males.
Males inherit their X chromosome from their father, who is more likely to carry the allele.
Recessive alleles on the X are copied more often during meiosis in males than in females.

why.correct: Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes: there is no second copy on the Y to mask a recessive allele. A female shows the trait only if both her X chromosomes carry it, which is much rarer.
options: With one X and no matching gene on the Y, one recessive allele is enough in a male.
The Y lacks most X genes; it does not carry a matching allele for this gene.
A son gets his X from his mother and his Y from his father.
DNA is copied once before meiosis in both sexes; copying does not depend on the allele.

items.q: Huntington's disease is autosomal dominant, and symptoms usually begin between ages 30 and 50. A man develops it at 45; his mother was never affected and lived to 85. His 20-year-old daughter has no symptoms. What is the probability that she carries the Huntington's allele?
options: 0, because she has no symptoms
1, because her father is affected

why.correct: His unaffected mother was hh, so he is Hh. His daughter's mother is unaffected (hh), so the daughter got H with probability 1/2. At 20, before the usual age of onset, having no symptoms tells us almost nothing.
options: Hh × hh gives Hh in half of the children, and her age means symptoms would not be expected yet.
1/4 would need two heterozygous parents and asks for hh; here one parent is Hh and the other hh.
With an allele whose effects begin in adulthood, a 20-year-old can carry it without symptoms.
Her father is heterozygous, so he passes H to half his children, not to every child.

items.q: Which event in meiosis is the physical basis of the law of segregation?
options: Homologs separate in anaphase I, so each gamete gets one allele of each gene.
Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II, so each gamete gets two identical alleles.
Homologs swap pieces in prophase I, so alleles move between chromosomes.
DNA is copied before meiosis, so each allele is present twice.

why.correct: The two alleles of a gene sit on the two homologs. When the homologs go to opposite poles in meiosis I, the alleles go to different cells, which is segregation.
options: Separating homologs separates the two alleles a diploid cell carries.
Sister chromatids carry identical alleles, and each gamete ends with one chromatid, so one allele.
Crossing over makes new combinations of alleles of different genes; segregation is about the two alleles of one gene.
Copying makes identical sister chromatids; it does not separate the two different alleles.

items.q: Select the condition that, by itself, makes two genes assort independently in Mendel's sense.
options: The two genes are on different chromosome pairs.
Each gene has one dominant and one recessive allele.
The two genes affect related traits, such as seed color and seed coat color.
The parents in the P generation are true-breeding.
The F1 plants are self-pollinated rather than crossed with each other.

why.correct: Independent assortment follows from separate homologous pairs lining up independently at metaphase I. Dominance, the traits involved and the way the parents were bred do not affect it.
options: Separate chromosome pairs line up independently, so their alleles sort independently.
Dominance affects how a genotype looks, not how alleles are sorted into gametes.
What the genes do does not matter; where they are on the chromosomes does.
True-breeding parents give a uniform F1, but the sorting happens in the F1's meiosis.
Selfing and crossing F1 plants give the same F2 when the F1 all have the same genotype.

items.q: Segregation and independent assortment explain inheritance in peas, fruit flies, yeast and humans, and all of these use DNA in chromosomes that are shared out by meiosis. What do these shared mechanisms most strongly suggest?
options: They share common ancestry and inherited the same machinery from it.
Each group evolved its own meiosis that happens to follow the same rules.
Pea plants were the first organisms, and the other groups descend from them.
Mendel's laws apply to plants, and animals copy them by learning.

why.correct: Complex shared mechanisms are most simply explained by descent from a common ancestor that already had them.
options: Shared, detailed machinery is evidence of common ancestry.
Several independent origins of the same detailed system is far less likely than one shared origin.
Shared features point to a shared ancestor, not to one living group being the ancestor of the others.
Inheritance is not learned; it works through chromosomes in every generation.

items.q: Put the steps of a monohybrid experiment like Mendel's in order.
options: Grow plants that are true-breeding for each form of the trait.
Cross the two true-breeding types (P generation).
Record that every F1 plant shows one form of the trait.
Self-pollinate the F1 plants.
Count the F2 plants of each form and find a ratio near 3:1.

why.correct: True-breeding parents are needed first; their cross gives a uniform F1; selfing the F1 gives the F2, whose counts show the 3:1 ratio.

items.q: In fruit flies, white eyes (w) is X-linked recessive to red eyes. Cross 1: a red-eyed (homozygous) female × a white-eyed male. Cross 2: a white-eyed female × a red-eyed male. Compared with cross 1, predict each value for the offspring of cross 2.

variables.name: Fraction of sons with white eyes
variables.why: Sons get their X from the mother. In cross 2 she has only X<sup>w</sup>, so every son is white-eyed; in cross 1 none are.

variables.name: Fraction of daughters with white eyes
variables.why: In both crosses each daughter gets one red allele (from the father in cross 2, the mother in cross 1), so no daughters are white-eyed.

variables.name: Fraction of daughters who carry the white allele
variables.why: In both crosses every daughter gets exactly one X<sup>w</sup>: from the father in cross 1, from the mother in cross 2.

variables.name: Fraction of all offspring with red eyes
variables.why: Cross 1 gives red eyes in every fly; cross 2 gives red-eyed daughters and white-eyed sons, so only half.

why.correct: For an X-linked gene, which parent carries the allele matters, because sons get their only X from their mother. Swapping the parents' phenotypes changes the sons' results but not the daughters'.
